content.thinking:
I'm putting the postmortem together from the key facts: the legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off at 06:29:33, and the monthly-spend feature turned on at that same moment. Reverting monthly-spend is ruled out, while reverting the fallback is confirmed. The page errors are a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 on account pages, and I'm checking whether those pages were served by the legacy or new renderer, since the new one usually returns 0.

I'm tracing the chain from the flag change back through the renderer switch to the division error. The fallback being switched off moved account pages onto the new renderer, which raises the ZeroDivisionError. That step rests only on the reading of the average-spend function, so I still need a run to confirm it.

I'm checking whether the new renderer's account pages actually reach the average-spend figure at line 47, since the log shows the error and the function explains it. The mechanism, an empty purchase list for shoppers with no purchases this month, rests on that function reading alone, and I have no run confirming it. I'm also noting that turning monthly-spend off didn't help, and no deploy appears before the incident.

I'm weighing whether a deploy could explain this, and the record shows none in the day before, since the rollout converged on one revision. I'm also ruling out the monthly-spend flag: turning it off changed nothing, and the fault persisted with it on, so it isn't needed to explain the incident.

I'm settling how to cite the failing line: the error sits at line {F1.1} of the spend-summary module, and I'll reference it by that figure rather than writing the number out. The file path itself has no digits, so it can stay as written, and the PR label gets treated as a name.

I'm drafting the postmortem's symptom and causal chain now, starting with shoppers whose account page requests failed, backed by the error evidence in the logs.

I'm tracing why account pages reached that code: after the legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off, they were served by the new renderer, which returned the highest share of requests in the window, and turning the fallback back on restored service.

I'm settling the last step of the chain: the pages the new renderer serves reach the per-item monthly spend figure, which divides by this month's purchase count, so shoppers who bought before but not this month hit a division by zero.

I'm writing the root-cause sentence now: the new account-page renderer reaches the per-item monthly spend function, which divides by this month's purchase count with no guard, so shoppers who bought before but not this month hit a ZeroDivisionError and their account page fails.

I'm drafting the cause-in-plain-words line next: a setting that kept account pages on the older version was switched off, sending shoppers to a newer version that likely fails when averaging this month's spend for anyone with no purchases this month. I'm also noting that switching the fallback off again would put the same failure back in front of account pages.

I'm listing the contributing factors now, starting with the missing pre-change check: the flag was switched to the new renderer for all traffic at once, with no staged rollout or error-rate gate visible in the record.

I'm listing the contributing factors, and one of them is the simultaneous flag flips: both were made in the same instant, so the first revert targeted the wrong flag and lengthened the response. I'm also noting that nobody was paged, which is a finding of its own, separate from whether it would have shortened the incident.

I'm weighing whether a missing paging link belongs among the contributing factors, but nobody being paged is better treated as a detection gap in what went wrong, since a person's arrival wouldn't clearly have shortened the incident. The lead was right and I'd weighed it without verifying it, so I'm recording that under went wrong as well.

I'm noting the went-well items: the investigator pinned the onset to the minute of the change, Argus undid its refuted revert, and the mitigation agent's revert of the fallback restored service, with a draft fix put up afterward. On the other side, nobody was paged, and the first action hit the wrong flag even though the thread's lead named the right one.

I'm writing up the action items now, starting with a prevention item for staged rollouts of flag changes that move account pages onto the new renderer.

I'm sorting out the last of the action items: staged rollouts for flag changes that move account pages onto the new renderer, plus a test run of that path before the switch, both aimed at the missing check. I'm also making sure the two flag changes don't happen in the same instant again, so each effect can be told apart.

I'm adding a detection item: routing the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to page the on-call rotation. I'm also noting that the log warning about account page error rates is supporting context rather than a separate cause. Then I'm recording the assumptions: the link from the new renderer to the line 47 function is inferred from log timing and the Code-Fix reading, not traced, and the claim that the errors came from shoppers with no purchases this month rests on that same reading. For the missing-check factor, a test on an account with past purchases but none this month would likely have shown the failure before shoppers saw it.

I'm pinning down the evidence for ruling out the monthly-spend feature: it was switched on at the same moment as the fallback, but the error persisted after it was switched off at 06:37:06. I'm also noting that the deploy check came back empty, with every replica on a single revision.

I'm writing the symptom step now: account page requests were failing, and the account-page error rate warning peaked at its highest point in the window.

I'm filling in the account-page step: those requests raised a ZeroDivisionError at line 47 of spend_summary.py over the logged window, and the requests failed. Next I'm checking the chain from the new renderer to that function, which divides by this month's purchase count and so fails for any shopper with none.

I'm noting the went-well items: the investigator pinned the start of the incident to the minute the two flag changes came in, Argus pulled the flag provider's history showing both changes, and the mitigation agent put monthly-spend-feature back on once reverting it was refuted, so the failed action wasn't left in place. The fallback revert restored service, and a draft fix went up afterward.

action_items.item: Before a flag is switched in production, require a test run of the code path it turns on. For legacy-checkout-fallback, that means the new renderer serving an account with past purchases but none this month.
Roll out flag changes that move account pages between renderers in stages, with an automatic halt and revert when the account-page error rate rises.
Make production flag changes on io-shop one at a time, with enough time between them to tell their effects apart.
Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account pages failed: account page requests came back as failed pages, and the logged account-page error rate peaked at {Gbac1.7}.
Account page requests raised a ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1} of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py over {G5309.3}, and each request that raised it failed.

ruled_out.what: The switch-on of monthly-spend-feature at {P2.1}, made at the same instant (candidate C1). Turning that flag back off left the service at the incident's level, so the flag was put back on.
A deploy. The deploy search over the day before came back empty, and all replicas ran one revision.

causal_chain.step: At {P1.1} the flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off, and account pages moved from the legacy renderer to the new one. At {G7ad6.6}, {G7ad6.1} of the flag's evaluations read off. Over {G7037.4} every evaluation read off. The new renderer's count of account pages served was highest at {Gc27d.11}, after being typically {Gc27d.10} before.

Pages served by the new renderer reach average_spend_per_item_this_month, which, as Code-Fix reads it, divides by the number of purchases made this month and so fails for any shopper who has bought nothing this month.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Someone turned off a setting that kept account pages on their older version, which sent shoppers to a newer version that likely breaks when it works out an average of this month's spending for anyone who has bought nothing this month.

contributing_factors.factor: Before legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off in production, no check was seen that the new renderer serves an account with past purchases but none this month.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Such a check would likely have failed before the flag was switched, and shoppers would never have reached the failing path.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag change moved all account-page traffic to the new renderer at once. Every evaluation read off from the minute after the switch, and no staged rollout or automatic halt on rising errors was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A staged switch with a halt on rising errors would have limited the failures to a small share of shoppers and turned the flag back sooner.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: legacy-checkout-fallback and monthly-spend-feature were changed by the same admin at the same instant, and the error named the spend-summary code. That made it hard to tell which change caused the failures.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: With the changes made apart, the onset would have pointed at the fallback flag alone, and the first revert would have been the one that worked, so the incident would have been shorter.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

lead_effects.effect: It did not change what was done: the lead was weighed as unverified, monthly-spend-feature was reverted first, and the flag it named was turned back on only after that revert was refuted, as the Investigator's second candidate.

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent placed the start of the incident at the minute the two flag changes came in.
Argus read the flag provider's history, which showed both flag changes by someone other than Argus.
The Mitigation Agent put monthly-spend-feature back on once turning it off was refuted, so an action that did not help was not left in place.
The Mitigation Agent turned legacy-checkout-fallback back on, and that brought the service back to normal.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged. No on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was called in to work it.

The investigation ranked monthly-spend-feature above legacy-checkout-fallback because the error named the spend-summary code, so the first revert went to the wrong flag. Yet the new renderer's count at the onset matched the fallback flag's off evaluations, and the thread had named the fallback flag.

input.root_cause: Switching legacy-checkout-fallback off sent account pages to the new renderer, and those pages reach average_spend_per_item_this_month in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. Code-Fix read that function as dividing this month's spend total by the number of purchases made this month, with nothing to handle a month with no purchases. So for any shopper who has bought before but not this month, the division raises ZeroDivisionError and the account page fails.
input.still_at_risk: If legacy-checkout-fallback is switched off again, the new renderer would serve account pages again, and they would fail for shoppers who have bought nothing this month.
input.symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
